items.title: Let the result come back: async routing and ownership in dsh-peer
items.summary: The previous post covered choosing a session. The real problem appeared afterwards: how does the result get back to whoever sent the message? This post records the final design — asynchronous result routing — and the bugs found along the way. None of them are exotic, but each one made the whole link look completely dead.
items.content_html:
The previous post covered choosing a session. The real problem appeared afterwards: how does the result get back to whoever sent the message?

This post records the final design — asynchronous result routing — and the bugs found along the way. None of them are exotic, but each one made the whole link look completely dead.

1. Final shape

No blocking, no polling, and no dependency on the hub agent remembering to reply.

2. Ownership: the hub cannot write into GUI sessions

The least intuitive constraint. In DSH every agent has an owner:

  • a GUI session's agent is created and held by the GUI session controller
  • the peer plugin's agents.get(id) returns nothing, and resume fails too

So "deliver into the session the user is watching" is not possible from a plugin. The solution is a session the hub creates itself:

Peer messages default there, its agent runs a turn, and the result is pushed back to macmini. A dedicated mailroom for peer traffic.

3. steer or prompt

The remote side may be running or idle when the result arrives:

Remote state Mechanism Effect
running session/steer injected at the next step; polling stops
idle session/prompt starts a turn with [hub] as input

Cached status is not trustworthy (session.status notifications never arrived), so query the link:

4. The real bugs

Symptom Root cause Fix
macmini never receives results const sessionId = agent.session.id inside #deliverToAgent shadowed the parameter, so remoteSessionId became the local id local id only as the map key; keep the remote id
new session throws unknown peer session working-directory/set called before the session exists ignore the error; the new session takes its cwd from peer/prepare-session
hub finds no agent, messages land in pending ownership isolation: GUI sessions are not writable deliver to a hub-owned Peer Inbox
results always take the prompt path and queue cached session.status stays idle forever query session/state before pushing
busy sessions wait for the whole turn followup only queues steer when running

The first bug is the archetype: it throws nothing, delivery works, but the push targets a session that does not exist. From the outside the link simply "does not answer".

5. How to verify

Do not trust "it should work now". Leave evidence:

And what macmini actually received:

Push log on one side, received text on the other — that is a closed loop.

6. The cost of initiator-side choice

"Whoever initiates chooses the target" was the agreed direction:

  • the link asks its local user which hub session to use
  • without targetSessionId a card appears; if nobody answers, the send is cancelled

That is correct for interactive use but blocking for unattended work. Mitigations: remember the last choice, or default to a well-known target such as peer-inbox.

7. What was removed

An intermediate peer_ask_hub tool sent a message and waited synchronously for the hub turn's text. It duplicated the async push and:

  • blocked the caller
  • waited forever when the hub session was busy
  • could deadlock if the hub called back synchronously

It was removed. Prefer async unless you truly need a reply in the same call.

8. Lessons

  • Understand ownership first: a plugin can only write to sessions it owns
  • The push id must be the remote id: a same-named local variable is a disaster
  • Do not trust cached status: one session/state call beats notification bookkeeping
  • Confirm the process really restarted: a scheduled restart silently did not run, and an old process wasted a long test
  • Add the log first: peer-push.log turned a mystery into one line of failure

items.title: Putting the choice on a session: interactive binding in dsh-peer
items.summary: The previous post covered steer and cancel. This one is about a different question: when the other side sends a message, which session should receive it — and when I send, which remote workspace and session should it target? The first version injected messages into "the session that last called the peer". That is neither predictable nor explainable. It is now a user choice, and the choice is enforced inside the tool rather than left to the model. 中文版: 让选择落到会话上
items.content_html:
The previous post covered steer and cancel. This one is about a different question: when the other side sends a message, which session should receive it — and when I send, which remote workspace and session should it target?

The first version injected messages into "the session that last called the peer". That is neither predictable nor explainable. It is now a user choice, and the choice is enforced inside the tool rather than left to the model.

中文版: 让选择落到会话上

1. Why choose a session at all

The early flow:

Three problems:

  • When several local sessions talked to the same peer, the last caller wins and the reply may land in the wrong conversation.
  • A peer session the hub never prompted has no caller, so the message falls back to a global guess.
  • The remote side may have dozens of sessions; the user has no idea where a message will land.

So the target becomes explicit: workspace + session.

2. Sending: one card, two questions

  1. peer_targets(peer) returns the remote side's workspaces and all sessions (live and persisted), with titles and directories.
  2. The tool calls userQuestions.ask with two questions:
    • remote workspace: existing workspaces, or a new directory typed by the user
    • remote session: existing sessions (title · directory), or a new session name
  3. Only after the answer does the tool continue with remoteDir and remoteSessionId.

The important part: this happens inside the tool's execute. peer_ask/peer_send await pickRemoteTarget(...) before hub.ask; without an answer, no send happens. The model cannot skip it — unless it passes remoteDir plus session/remoteSessionId explicitly (the operations path).

3. Receiving: pending first, then bind

Details:

  • No automatic injection: the message waits in pending until the user decides.
  • Durable: enqueue and bind both write the file, so a hub restart does not lose the queue.
  • Stale notices: after a successful bind, a late notice checks peer_pending first; when the id is gone it answers "already handled" instead of asking again.

4. Why the remote session is not visible in the GUI

The remote Web GUI lists sessions by workspace, filtered by the session header's cwd. Peer sessions were originally created with the link's default directory:

The fix has two parts:

  1. Before creating a session, the hub sends peer/prepare-session with the chosen directory, and the link uses it as the header cwd.
  2. After creation, the link finds the workspace with that path (creating it if needed) and calls attachSession.

Existing sessions keep their old header cwd; only new sessions land in the chosen workspace.

5. Where session titles come from

Session state Title source
live (in the link process) sessionTitle.get(session).title
persisted but not open the title projection in sessionProjectionCache.cachedSnapshot(header)

The list is merged, sorted by createdAt descending, capped at 30; the card shows the most recent 8.

6. Pitfalls along the way

Symptom Cause Fix
No existing sessions in the card the hub listed only its in-memory link.sessions, empty after a restart ask the link via peer/sessions and merge persisted sessions
Chose a directory, remote still ran in the old one working-directory/set changes the projection, not the header; the SDK server's ctx.workingDirectory needs an injection the link implements set itself and uses peer/prepare-session before creation
The card appeared even with explicit arguments the picker was unconditional skip it when remoteDir + session/remoteSessionId are provided
Pending messages vanished after a restart in-memory queue persist to peer-pending.json
A stale notice asked again after binding the notice was already queued check pending first; empty means "already handled"

7. Still missing

  • A native in-app picker: the choice is rendered by userQuestions.ask (two questions on one card), not a dedicated session-picker component.
  • Code-level permissions: peer-origin turns still run with the user session's authority; they should use a restricted preset with human approval for privileged actions.
  • Header migration: old sessions cannot change their header cwd; only new sessions get the chosen workspace.

8. Takeaways

  • Make the target explicit: workspace and session are chosen, not inferred.
  • Enforce inside the tool, not in the prompt: userQuestions.ask in execute cannot be skipped by the model.
  • Visibility needs header cwd + workspace attach, not just "create a session".
  • Cross-process state such as pending must be durable, or one restart loses it.

items.title: Adding steer and cancel to a two-agent channel: preemptive interjection inside DeepSeek Harness
items.summary: The previous post covered dsh-peer's connection direction and activity dashboard. This one goes after a narrower question: how do you interject while the other agent is in the middle of a turn, and even abort it? It took a while to see that DSH has three granularities of "sending a message": prompt, steer, and cancel. The difference is not in the network layer — it is in the agent loop's turn/step boundaries. 中文版: 给两个 agent 的对话加上 steer 与 cancel
items.content_html:
The previous post covered dsh-peer's connection direction and activity dashboard. This one goes after a narrower question: how do you interject while the other agent is in the middle of a turn, and even abort it?

It took a while to see that DSH has three granularities of "sending a message": prompt, steer, and cancel. The difference is not in the network layer — it is in the agent loop's turn/step boundaries.

中文版: 给两个 agent 的对话加上 steer 与 cancel

1. A peer call is really a tool call

To the model, peer_ask is an ordinary tool:

The remote side is a full runtime with its own model, tools, and session, but here it is wrapped as a function from prompt to final text. That abstraction has three gaps: no streaming, no reverse question, and no preemption. The first two were patched with a session mirror and an inbox; this post is about the third.

2. How one turn actually runs

A turn consists of multiple steps; each step is one LLM request plus tool execution:

Before each step the driver claims messages from the inbox, which has two queues:

Queue Written by Consumed
next-turn prompt / followup after the current turn, as the first input of the next turn
next-step steer / inject before the next step starts, inside the current turn

Details that are easy to miss:

  • steer does not interrupt the current step — running tools finish; the message is seen at the next step
  • steer can keep a turn alive — if the model already decided to stop but next-step still has messages, the loop opens another step instead of breaking
  • cancel keeps the queue — with keepInbox: true, queued steers survive for a later turn
  • the inbox is durable — it is a session projection written into the session log, so it survives a restart

So the three granularities are:

3. Protocol design

Three wire methods served by the link's PeerHarnessServer:

Method Params Result
session/steer { sessionId, contentBlocks } { accepted, messageId }
session/cancel { sessionId, reason? } { cancelled, status }
session/state { sessionId } { status, seq }

The link-side implementation is short; the important line is the ownership check — it only touches sessions this server created:

The hub routes and rate-limits:

Two more constraints:

  • Version gate: links older than 0.3.0 get a prompt fallback for steer, and cancel fails loudly instead of hitting an unknown method
  • Rate limit: 20 steer/cancel calls per peer per minute (steerPerMinute)

4. Why a reverse question always arrives a turn late

The hub's answer goes out as session/prompt, and the SDK server turns that into:

followup lands in next-turn, so the answer is queued for the link's next turn:

  • peer_ask / peer_send are just how the hub sends its answer; they are not a status query
  • the answer becomes a user message in the link's next turn
  • the link gets a delivery receipt, not the answer itself

A true request/response needs either a suspended RPC or a link-side inbox plus peer_wait.

5. Where the three granularities sit

6. The actual steer / cancel test

After macmini upgraded to 0.3.0:

The link stayed connected afterwards:

Two semantics to keep in mind:

  1. steer's "delivered" means queued. While the 90-second command was still running, the message sat in next-step; the model would only see it after that step. We cancelled right after, so it stayed in the queue under keepInbox: true and will be consumed in the next turn — not lost.
  2. cancel aborts the turn, not the process. The running shell command may still finish; the agent stops advancing.

7. The bug the test caught: a missing import

macmini kept reporting silent handshake failures. It looked like a network issue, but it was one import:

link.js used PEER_VERSION in status(), peer/hello, and reconnect state, but only hub.js imported it. Every dial threw a ReferenceError inside the handshake try/catch, was recorded as "handshake failed", and retried with backoff — the real exception never reached the log.

Fix: 38f6c10 on feat/session-mirror.

The lesson matters more than the fix: on a cross-machine link, any error swallowed by a catch looks like a network problem. Keep the original exception at least at the handshake boundary.

8. What is still missing

  • Code-level permission enforcement: peer-origin messages are still plain user messages, and a peer-woken turn runs with the user session's authority. The next step is to pin peer-origin turns to a restricted preset and require human approval for privileged actions.
  • Link-side inbox / wait: a link can send, but cannot wait for the hub's answer within the same turn.
  • Durable provenance: carry origin on the wire and store it in the message source instead of relying on a text prefix.

9. Takeaways

  • prompt / steer / cancel differ at the turn/step boundary, not on the wire
  • steer is "next step", not an interrupt; cancel aborts the activity, not the process
  • a version gate and a rate limit are part of the protocol, not polish
  • when a cross-machine link misbehaves, suspect a swallowed exception before the network

Code:

  • SparksDing/dsh-peer (feat/session-mirror)
  • fork: SparksDing/deepseek-harness (feat/peer-session-mirror)

items.title: Let Two DeepSeek Harness Instances Talk Across Machines: dsh-peer's Backend and Activity Dashboard
items.summary: I recently built something small but useful: a channel that lets a DeepSeek Harness (dsh) instance on Linux and another on Windows talk to each other — not "SSH in and run a command", but two agents delegating turns and messaging each other. The result is a plugin called dsh-peer, plus an activity dashboard that shows the remote agent's thinking as it happens. Code: SparksDing/dsh-peer. This post covers the design, the interaction flow, and why the dashboard lives inside the bridge. 中文版: 让两个 DeepSeek Harness 跨机器对话
items.content_html:
I recently built something small but useful: a channel that lets a DeepSeek Harness (dsh) instance on Linux and another on Windows talk to each other — not "SSH in and run a command", but two agents delegating turns and messaging each other. The result is a plugin called dsh-peer, plus an activity dashboard that shows the remote agent's thinking as it happens.

Code: SparksDing/dsh-peer. This post covers the design, the interaction flow, and why the dashboard lives inside the bridge.

中文版: 让两个 DeepSeek Harness 跨机器对话

1. Background and constraints

dsh ships an SDK protocol over stdio: a parent process spawns dsh --profile sdk and speaks JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout. There is no cross-machine channel.

Three real constraints shaped the design:

  1. Windows sits behind NAT. It can only make outbound connections.
  2. The Linux side's inbound ports are blocked by the cloud security group; only HTTP-ish ports such as 80/3080 are reachable.
  3. The thing being driven is not a bare tool process but a complete runtime: its own model route, tool set, session persistence, and filesystem.

So the goal was explicit: reuse dsh's SDK protocol and add a "cross-machine + symmetric" layer without touching the core.

2. Architecture: connection direction and service direction are opposite

This is the easiest part to get confused about, and the most important:

Establishes the connection Sends harness requests Responds
hub (public side) listens yes (session/prompt) only peer/reply
link (private side) dials no serves harness methods

NAT only allows the private machine to dial out, so Windows must be the "connection client" — while it is simultaneously the "capability server", exposing its local agent to the hub.

The stack is straightforward:

3. Protocol: reuse the SDK dialect

3.1 Frames and transport

Every frame is one line of JSON-RPC 2.0: method + id is a request, id alone is a response, method alone is a notification. This matches @deepseek-ai/dsh-sdk-protocol, so both ends already understand the harness methods:

  • initialize: cwd, provider, model
  • session/prompt: enqueue one user message
  • session/wait, session/working-directory/*
  • notifications: session.event, session.status

Only four methods are custom: peer/hello, peer/ping, peer/info, peer/reply, plus peer/ensure-session for compatibility.

Transport is pluggable because the same JSON-RPC only needs a Duplex:

3.2 Handshake

The first request from a link is:

The hub checks the protocol version and compares the token in constant time, refusing anything that does not match. After that:

  • an application-level peer/ping every 25 seconds, dropping the connection after two consecutive misses;
  • on disconnect, the link reconnects with exponential backoff from 1s up to 30s.

3.3 One peer_ask, end to end

One subtle implementation detail: the hub does not use session/wait to detect the end of a turn. The 0.2.0 SDK server only implements initialize, session/prompt, and shutdown. Instead, the hub keeps per-session state on each connection:

  • receipts: messageIds confirmed by agent/inbox/spliced
  • idleCount: how many times session.status became idle
  • lastAssistant: text of the last assistant message

The wait condition is "idleCount increased since before the prompt", not "wait for an idle notification" — the latter loses the event when the turn finishes before the wait starts.

3.4 Session identity and continuity

Session ids are peer-<link>-<topic>:

  • reusing a session name continues the same conversation; fresh: true starts a new one;
  • after a reconnect the hub re-runs initialize, then peer/ensure-session for existing conversations;
  • the link first tries session/resume to load persisted history; if that fails (first use), the next prompt creates it.

Conversations therefore survive restarts of either side.

3.5 Event filtering

HarnessSdkJsonRpcServer broadcasts session.event for every session in the runtime. For a peer channel that is both wasteful and a privacy leak, so the link wraps the transport:

owned is populated when session/prompt or session/resume arrives, so only sessions created by this peer connection are forwarded.

4. Backend details worth noting

4.1 Tools come from agent presets, not the global plane

Mounting the link in the web profile hits a snag: peer sessions only see globally registered tools (peer_reply, peer_status) — no bash, read, or write, because the Web profile moves every model-facing tool row into an agent preset.

The fix is to subclass HarnessSdkJsonRpcServer and override createSession so the preset is mounted in the pre-publication setup hook:

setup runs before the agent is published, so the preset's tools exist when the first prompt is assembled.

4.2 Older versions have no session/resume

0.2.0's SDK server exposes only three methods, and agents.create on an existing session id fails with session "..." already exists. The compatibility path catches that and falls back to agents.resume:

4.3 When only an HTTP port is reachable: WebSocket plus a bridge

The public side's 3099 is blocked by the security group, but 3080 works (nginx). So one path was added:

The bridge is tiny: it accepts the WebSocket upgrade and pipes each connection to the hub's TCP port. The hub stays unchanged and keeps listening on raw TCP.

nginx needs one exact-match location that does not disturb the dsh GUI:

4.4 Binary artifacts get a separate upload endpoint

The protocol carries JSON text only. Pushing screenshots or preview QR codes through JSON-RPC (base64) is expensive and fragile, so there is a small token-checked upload endpoint:

On the remote side, Invoke-WebRequest -Method Put -InFile is enough.

5. Frontend: the activity dashboard

5.1 Why it lives in the bridge

The requirement was to see the remote agent's thinking and details: user messages, reasoning, assistant text, tool calls and results, turn boundaries, status changes.

The obvious approach — a dsh client UI plugin — has two problems:

  1. Its data plane needs typert Remote descriptors, which are generated at build time; out-of-tree plugins have a hard time wiring that up.
  2. More importantly, adding a read-only panel should not require restarting the hub that is already running.

The WebSocket bridge happens to sit between the link and the hub and sees every JSON-RPC frame. So the dashboard was implemented there: the bridge parses frames on the side, feeds an in-memory store, and serves a minimal HTTP page.

Neither the hub nor the link changed.

5.2 Event model

dsh session events are a discriminated union. The dashboard keeps the ones worth showing:

Event Display
user/message user or injected message text
assistant/message split into reasoning and text blocks
tool/call tool name + argument JSON
tool/result result text, red when isError
turn/start / turn/end turn boundaries and end reason
session.status running / idle

Each event is flattened into a ring buffer:

seq is globally monotonic, which makes incremental fetching trivial.

5.3 Incremental polling

No push channel — just polling every 900 ms with a since cursor:

Only events with seq > since come back, so responses stay small. The server keeps the last 400 events per session and 4000 overall, dropping the oldest from the least recently active session.

Polling instead of SSE is a pragmatic choice: a dashboard is usually watched briefly, and failure recovery (refresh, reconnect) costs almost no code.

5.4 Rendering

The page is one self-contained HTML string with no external assets and no frontend build step — a function returns it directly:

Rendering groups by session; new events are appended to the end. The header shows a peer status dot (green when any session is running), and an optional "follow" checkbox keeps the view scrolled to the bottom.

The result is a chronological stream: purple for reasoning, yellow for tool calls, green for results, red for failures, gray for turn boundaries.

5.5 Security

The dashboard runs on the public 3080, so:

  • both the page and the JSON endpoint require a token query parameter;
  • the page embeds that token into its fetches;
  • the bridge is read-only and exposes no write endpoint.

6. Real-world validation

This was not a paper design; it ran end to end on real machines:

  1. Windows runs dsh --profile sdk as a link and connects to the Linux hub over ws://…/dsh-peer;
  2. on Linux, peer_ask(peer="HP", prompt="check disk") makes the Windows agent run pwsh and return the result;
  3. the agent then drives WeChat DevTools through miniprogram-automator, reads page elements, takes screenshots, and uploads the preview QR code and screenshots back through the upload endpoint;
  4. the dashboard shows its reasoning, tool calls, and results step by step.

Pitfalls worth recording:

  • Web profile tools live in presets, and only peer tools are global;
  • 0.2.0 has no session/resume, so reconnects must fall back to agents.resume;
  • HMR only replaces plugin files inside the profile directory; new files outside it are not hot-loaded — which is why the bridge became a standalone process;
  • The Windows sandbox requires temp to be outside the workspace; when the workspace is the home directory, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp is inside it and startup is refused;
  • The WeChat DevTools CLI writes to %LOCALAPPDATA%, so a workspace outside the home directory blocks it; its service port must be enabled manually, and preview requires a real AppID (touristappid fails with "AppID does not exist").

7. Limitations and next steps

  • The link agent is event-driven: it runs only when prompted. It can interject with peer_reply during a turn, but cannot start one on its own.
  • The dashboard only covers links that go through the bridge; a direct TCP link would need the same recording logic inside the hub.
  • With multiple users or machines, events would need subscriptions and per-peer permissions (today the token is all-or-nothing).
  • Embedding the panel inside the dsh Web GUI would need a client plugin plus typert descriptors — significantly more work, so it stays a standalone page for now.

8. Code

  • Repository: SparksDing/dsh-peer
  • Backend: lib/protocol.js, lib/hub.js, lib/link.js, lib/link-server.js
  • Transport: lib/transport.js, lib/ws.js
  • Dashboard: lib/activity.js (event model + HTML), bin/peer-ws-bridge.mjs (side parsing + HTTP endpoints)
  • Tests: node test/hub.test.mjs, node test/tools.test.mjs (no model and no dsh required)

If the approach is useful to you, take it and adapt it. Issues about better observability are welcome — especially "how to observe a process without modifying it".
